   PUBLIC RULES OF DECORUM
In compliance with the Ralph M. Brown Act and to further facilitate feedback, public comment is
encouraged at meetings of the City Council, its Authorities, Agencies, and Boards and Commissions, and
Committees and its Agencies, in accordance with the following rules. Please note Members of the
public are encouraged to contact the City Manager, or respective Operating Department Directors, first
before making service requests or service complaints directly to the Council.

    At the beginning of each meeting to consider Closed Session items, public comments are
  permitted to address one (1) or more Closed Session Items scheduled on the Agenda prior to the
  Inglewood City Council convening deliberations in private. Public comments during Closed
  Session shall not exceed a total of one (1) minute in length.

    At the beginning of each meeting to consider Open Session items (Consent Calendar, Warrants
  and Bills, Setting Public Hearings, Departmental Reports, Authority and Agency Items, Council
  Initiatives, etc.), public comments are permitted to address one (1) or more Open Session Items
  (excluding Closed Session Items, and Public Hearings) scheduled on the Agenda. Public
  Comments occurring at the beginning of Open Session shall not exceed a total of three (3)
  minutes in length.

    Public comments are not permitted on any scheduled Closed or Open Agenda item or Public
  Hearing in the event the item has been pulled from the Agenda, postponed or rescheduled for
  another date.

    Public comments to address a Public Hearing scheduled on the Agenda shall not to exceed 1
  minute in length.

    At the conclusion of the City Council meeting prior to adjournment, public comments are
  permitted on any items of interest to the public and within the subject matter jurisdiction of the
  City Council. Public comments occurring at the end of Open Session shall not to exceed one (1)
  minute in length.

    The Mayor, or Presiding Officer of the meeting may, at his or her discretion, restrict or grant
  additional speaker time based on such considerations as Agenda length, volume of speakers,
  complexity of item, or looming threat of loss of quorum.

    The Mayor, or Presiding Officer of the meeting may request that a spokesperson be chosen by
  the group to address the Council when a group of persons wish to comment on the same
  subject matter.

    Speakers are not permitted to cede their time, or any portion thereof, to another speaker.

    The Mayor, or Presiding Officer of the meeting, may invoke the use of speaker cards at any time
  use of such cards is deemed necessary to facilitate the orderly process of permitting public
  comment.
   All public comments are to be directed to the Mayor, or the Presiding Officer, and not to any
  other member of the public or to any single Council, Authority, Agency, Board, Commission, or
  Committee Member unless in response to a question from that Member.

  Any person making a public comment who wishes to provide written or other materials to the
  Mayor and Council must first request permission to approach the dais. If and when permission is
  granted, materials shall be given to the Sergeant At Arms for distribution.

  Commenters must be civil and respectful when addressing the Mayor and Council Members,
  and making reference to others.

  No person attending a public meeting shall engage in disorderly or boisterous
  conduct—including but not limited to applause, whistling, feet stamping, booing or making any
  loud, threatening, profane, abusive, personal, impertinent or slanderous uttering or comments.
  No person is allowed to disturb, disrupt, or otherwise impede the orderly conduct of the
  meeting.

  Members of the audience and speakers shall not wear or display signs, placards, banners, hats,
  costumes or similar items at any time in the Council Chamber that obstruct the view of the
  legislative body or audience members, or which creates sufficient disruption to impede the
  orderly conduct of the meeting or to intimidate other attendees of the meetings.

  Persons making public comment should not routinely expect to receive answers to questions
  posed during their remarks. Unlike Town Hall, Neighborhood Block, and other meetings and
  gatherings more conducive to question and answer format, City Council Meetings are business
  meetings. In many cases staff will be available to take speaker questions and contact
  information and respond in a timely manner.

  ENFORCEMENT OF RULES AND DECORUM
  The Mayor, or Presiding Officer of the Council or Committee, with the assistance of the
  Sergeant-at-Arms or any law enforcement officer, shall be responsible for maintaining the order
  of the meeting and uniformly enforcing the Rules of Decorum.

  In the event that any person breaches the Rules of Decorum, the Mayor, or Presiding Officer,
  shall order the person to cease the offending conduct.

  If any person continues to breach the Rules of Decorum in a manner that disturbs, disrupts or
  otherwise impedes the orderly conduct of the meeting following an order from the Mayor, or
  Presiding Officer, to cease the offending conduct, the Mayor, or Presiding Officer, may order
  that person to leave the meeting.

  If any person refuses to leave the public meeting following an order to do so from the Mayor or
  Presiding Officer, that person may be escorted out of the meeting by any law enforcement
  officer present and may be subject to arrest for violation of the California Penal Code or
  Inglewood Municipal Code.

1. A representative from the City Attorney’s Office gave a presentation about the Brown Act, Conflict of Interest,
  Inglewood Municipal Code 2-107 et seq. and how the mechanics of running a Commission meeting.

  a. Sunshine Law or the Brown Act
   This law covered public bodies to do their business publicly. Under the Act, all Commission meetings are
  open and public, and all persons are permitted to attend the meetings. Statutory exceptions authorizing closed
  sessions (few, if any, are available to this Commission) are construed narrowly, and the Brown Act “sunshine
  law” is construed liberally in favor of openness in conducting public business.
  b. Conflict of Interest
   The conflict of interest rules of the Political Reform Law state that local government must serve the needs and
  respond to the desires of all citizens equally, regardless of their wealth. Furthermore, public officials, whether
  elected or appointed, must perform their duties impartially, free from bias caused by their own financial
  interests or the financial interests of people who have supported them.
   Members of the Parking and Traffic Commission will not receive compensation for their services in the
  performance of their respective duties and functions as Commissioners.
  c. Meeting Operating Mechanism
   The Commission shall hold regular meetings at least once each calendar month, the time and place of which
  shall be fixed by resolution of the Commission.
   The Chairman or Chairperson of the Parking and Traffic Commission may call additional meetings in addition
  to directing the meetings. For example, the Chairperson can decide the length of time during public comments.
  The public is allowed to speak longer on any agenda item during Public Comments, but the time period must
  be managed by the Chair.
   The Chairperson should acknowledge anyone on the panel before speaking or responding to comments.

SUBJECT:  Update on the Request to Amend Residential Permit Parking Program for 3rd
  Avenue between 102nd Street and 104th Street within District 9

BACKGROUND:
In June 2020, the City Council adopted a Citywide Residential Permit Parking Program. The program is
enforced 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, with two-hour parking Monday through Sunday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.
(Ordinance No. 20-09). The program was adopted to protect residential communities more effectively
and efficiently from non-resident vehicle intrusion. On November 9, 2022, Public Works (PW)
Department received a petition requesting the removal of Residential Permit Parking on 3rd Avenue
between 102nd Street and 104th Street within District 9. There is a count of twenty (20) properties that
are within the limit. Sixteen (16) valid signatures (one signature per residential unit) were submitted on
the petition, resulting in eighty percent (80%) of all households on the block signing the petition in favor
of removing the permit parking restrictions. On October 4, 2023, a notice was sent to all addresses within
the petition boundary to attend the October Traffic and Parking Commission meeting to express their
views on the matter.

DISCUSSION:
On October 25, 2023, the Parking and Traffic Commission held a public hearing on the issue of
terminating the Residential Permit Parking Program for 3rd Avenue between 102nd Street and 104th
Street within District 9. The Public Works Department requested that the Parking and Traffic Commission
listen to public comments and provide direction on whether the petition should go to a vote by the
residents. As a result, all district commissioners voted to approve the request to begin the voting process.
On November 6, 2023, the Public Works Department mailed questionaries to each resident residing in
the boundary area of the petition and requested the questionnaires be returned within thirty (30) calendar
days. December 7, 2023 was the deadline for the City to accept responses to the questionnaires. On
December 12, 2023, the questionnaires were counted. Eight (8) votes were cast to approve the
termination, while three (3) votes opposed the termination of the Residential Permit Parking Program.

Based on the number of votes received, seventy-three percent (73%) of households supported the
approval to terminate the Residential Permit Parking Program on 3rd Avenue between 102nd Street and
104th Street within District 9. For the parking restrictions to be removed, a minimum of seventy-five
percent (75%) of the returned questionnaires must be in favor of the removal. Therefore, based on
residents' results, the process of terminating the Residential Permit Parking Program on 3rd Avenue
between 102nd and 104th Streets within District 9 will stop and no change will occur in the Residential
Permit Parking Program.

to state their opinion of the subject matter.

on-street (curbside) parking spaces within a neighborhood where the patrons and/or employees of a
nearby commercial or industrial facility are otherwise using all available on-street parking spaces.

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the Parking and Traffic Commission conduct a public hearing to do the following:
1. Receive Public Comments regarding the termination of the Residential Permit Parking Program on
  Christopher Avenue between Lemoli Avenue and approximately 132-ft South of 118th Place within
  District 11; and
2. Provide direction to the City Engineer on how to proceed

BACKGROUND:
In June 2020, the City Council adopted a Citywide Residential Permit Parking Program. The program is
enforced 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, with two-hour parking Monday through Sunday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.
(Ordinance No. 20-09). The program was adopted to protect residential communities more effectively
and efficiently from non-resident vehicle intrusion.

On August 29, 2023, Public Works (PW) Department received a petition requesting the removal of
Residential Permit Parking on Christopher Avenue between Lemoli Avenue and approximately 132-ft
South of 118th Place within District 11. There is a count of thirty-seven (37) properties that are within the
limit. Twenty-six (26) valid signatures (one signature per residential unit) were submitted on the petition,
resulting in seventy percent (70%) of all households on the block signing the petition in favor of removing
the permit parking restrictions. On January 9, 2024, a notice was sent to all addresses within the petition
boundary to attend the January Traffic and Parking Commission meeting to express their views on the
matter.

DISCUSSION:
The Residential Permit Parking District Program encourages residents to use their driveways to park their
vehicles, when available, so that those without driveways can park on the street. Therefore, Public Works
staff requests the Parking and Traffic Commission to provide instructions on how to proceed with the
request by either:
1. Approving the request to start the voting process; or
2. Denying the request to end the processing of the petition.

on-street (curbside) parking spaces within a neighborhood where the patrons and/or employees of a
nearby commercial or industrial facility are otherwise using all available on-street parking spaces.

would be warranted. If it is determined to be warranted, ballots will be mailed to each household within
the subject area.

If a Residential Permit Parking District is terminated, all residents and visitors in this neighborhood will
not be restricted from parking on the public streets at any time; including during special events. If you
have any questions regarding this matter, or wish to express an opinion but are unable to attend the

SUBJECT:  Request to Terminate Residential Permit Parking Program for 102nd Street and 7th

RECOMMENDATION:
It is requested that the Parking and Traffic Commission review the information included in this report and
approve the resolution to terminate the Residential Permit Parking Program within District 9 on 102nd
Street and 7th Avenue from Century Blvd Local Access to 104th Street.

BACKGROUND:
In June 2020, the City Council adopted a Citywide Residential Permit Parking Program. The program is
enforced 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, with two-hour parking Monday through Sunday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.
(Ordinance No. 20-09). The program was adopted to protect residential communities more effectively
and efficiently from non-resident vehicle intrusion.

On November 8, 2022, Public Works (PW) Department received a petition requesting the removal of
Residential Permit Parking on 102nd Street from 7th Avenue to 2nd Avenue. Due to the geometry of the
street and the addresses that signed the petition, the Department of Public Works recommended
including the transition of 102nd Street into 7th Avenue in the petition for 102nd Street from Century
Boulevard Local Access to 104th Street. There is a count of ninety-two (92) properties that are within
the limit.

Seventy-five (75) valid signatures (one signature per residential unit) were submitted on the petition,
resulting in eighty-two percent (82%) of all households on the block signing the petition in favor of
removing the permit parking restrictions. On September 8, 2023, a notice was sent to all addresses
within the petition boundary to attend the September Traffic and Parking Commission meeting to express
their views on the matter.

DISCUSSION:
On September 27, 2023, the Parking and Traffic Commission held a public hearing on the issue of
terminating the Residential Permit Parking Program for 102nd Street and 7th Avenue from Century Blvd
Local Access to 104th Street within District 9. The Public Works Department requested that the Parking
and Traffic Commission listen to public comments and provide direction on whether the petition should
go to a vote by the residents. As a result, all district commissioners voted to approve the request to begin
the voting process.

On October 5, 2023, the Public Works Department mailed questionaries to each resident residing in the
boundary area of the petition and requested the questionnaires be returned within thirty (30) calendar
days. November 8, 2023 was the deadline for the City to accept responses to the questionnaires. On
November 14, 2023, the questionnaires were counted. Fifty-two (52) votes were cast to approve the
termination, while nine (9) votes opposed the termination of the Residential Permit Parking Program.
Based on the number of votes received, eighty-five percent (85%) of households supported the approval
to terminate the Residential Permit Parking Program on 102nd Street and 7th Avenue from Century Blvd
Local Access to 104th Street within District 9.

Subject:  Vote to Approve or Reject the termination of residential permit parking on 102nd
  Street and 7th Avenue from Century Blvd Local Access to 104th Street within
  District 9

The purpose of this letter is to allow residents the opportunity to vote on the removal of the residential
permit parking for on 102nd Street and 7th Avenue from Century Blvd Local Access to 104th Street
within District 9.

By voting "approve", this street will not be subject to the rules of a Residential Permit Parking District.
By voting "reject", this street will continue to have permitted parking and follow the rules associated
with it. The complete rules and procedures can be found in the Inglewood Municipal Code Section 3-76
(Establishment of a Permit Parking District) through Section 3-76.1 (Amending or Terminating a Permit
Parking District).

Since the Parking and Traffic Commission has determined that permitted parking may not be warranted
in the area in question, ballots are mailed to all residences within the boundary of the subject street.

If seventy-five percent (75%) or more of the returned ballots vote “approve” for the termination of
residential permit parking, then an ordinance amending the Residential Permit Parking District will be
submitted to the City Council for consideration. If approved, on 102nd Street and 7th Avenue from
Century Blvd Local Access to 104th Street within District 9 will not be subject to the Residential Permit
Parking District rules. Therefore, all vehicles can park on these streets without showing a parking
permit at all hours of the day, every day of the week. Additionally, the current parking prohibitions for
street sweeping will remain unchanged.

Using the enclosed ballot, please vote to approve or reject the termination of the residential permit
parking on 102nd Street and 7th Avenue from Century Blvd Local Access to 104th Street within District
9. Please return the ballot to the City of Inglewood Public Works Department within thirty (30) days
from the date of this letter. Only one vote per household will be accepted. If you have any questions,
please do not hesitate to get in touch with the Public Works Department, at (310) 412-5333.

El propósito de esta carta es brindarles a los residentes la oportunidad de votar sobre la eliminación
del permiso de estacionamiento residencial en 102nd Street y 7th Avenue desde Century Blvd Local
Access hasta 104th Street dentro del Distrito 9.

Al votar "aprobar", esta calle no estará sujeta a las normas de un distrito de estacionamiento con
permiso residencial. Al votar "rechazar", esta calle seguirá teniendo estacionamiento permitido y
seguirá las reglas asociadas con ella. Las reglas y procedimientos completos se pueden encontrar
en el Código Municipal de Inglewood, Sección 3-76 (Establecimiento de un Distrito de
Estacionamiento con Permiso) hasta la Sección 3-76.1 (Modificación o Terminación de un Distrito
de Estacionamiento con Permiso).

Dado que la Comisión de Estacionamiento y Tráfico ha determinado que es posible que el
estacionamiento permitido no esté garantizado en el área en cuestión, las boletas se envían por
correo a todas las residencias dentro de los límites de la calle en cuestión. Si el setenta y cinco por
ciento (75%) o más de las boletas devueltas votan "aprobar" la terminación del permiso de
estacionamiento residencial, entonces se presentará al Concejo Municipal para su consideración
una ordenanza que modifica el Distrito de Estacionamiento con Permiso Residencial. Si se
aprueba, en 102nd Street y 7th Avenue desde Century Blvd, el acceso local hasta 104th Street
dentro del Distrito 9 no estará sujeto a las reglas del Distrito con Permiso de Estacionamiento
Residencial.

Por lo tanto, todos los vehículos pueden estacionar en estas calles sin mostrar un permiso de
estacionamiento a todas horas del día, todos los días de la semana. Además, las prohibiciones de
estacionamiento actuales para el barrido de calles se mantendrán sin cambios.
